content: Sarcomas are malignant tumors that originate in connective tissues, including those derived from bone, fat, and muscle. The muscular wall of the uterus, known as the myometrium, is primarily composed of smooth muscle. Cancers that arise from smooth muscle are referred to as leiomyosarcomas (LMSs). Among uterine sarcomas, LMSs are the most prevalent. However, compared to other forms of uterine cancer, LMSs are highly aggressive, with a significant risk of recurrence and mortality, regardless of the stage at diagnosis. LMSs are rare, with an incidence of approximately 9 cases per million individuals. The incidence increases rapidly after the age of 35 and plateaus in individuals aged 50 and older. Risk factors for LMS include nulliparity (having never given birth), advancing age, obesity, and a history of pelvic radiation. The symptoms of LMS often mimic those of benign uterine leiomyomas (fibroids), including abnormal vaginal bleeding, a palpable pelvic mass, and pelvic pain. The coexistence of fibroids and LMS can complicate the diagnostic process. LMSs can grow rapidly, potentially leading to tumor rupture and intra-abdominal bleeding. Locally advanced disease may cause symptoms due to invasion or compression of adjacent pelvic organs, such as hematuria (bleeding into the bladder) or ureteral obstruction (blockage of the tubes that drain the kidneys into the bladder). LMSs have a propensity for early hematogenous (bloodstream) spread to distant sites. Approximately 33% of patients with newly diagnosed uterine LMS present with distant metastatic disease (stage IVB), most commonly involving the liver, lungs, or upper abdomen. Diagnosis is often made retrospectively following surgical procedures such as hysterectomy (removal of the uterus) or myomectomy (removal of fibroids while preserving the uterus). This delay in diagnosis or misdiagnosis is common when conservative management is pursued for presumed fibroids. The staging of uterine LMS is based on the 2009 FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system for uterine sarcomas, which also includes endometrial stromal sarcoma and uterine adenosarcoma. However, this staging system has limited utility in predicting survival outcomes. The stages are as follows: Stage IA: Tumor confined to the uterus, measuring <5 cm. Stage IB: Tumor confined to the uterus, measuring >5 cm. Stage IIA: Tumor extends to the pelvis with adnexal involvement. Stage IIB: Tumor extends to extra-uterine pelvic tissues. Stage IIIA: Tumor invades abdominal tissues at one site. Stage IIIB: Tumor invades abdominal tissues at multiple sites. Stage IIIC: Metastasis to pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes. Stage IVA: Tumor invades the bladder and/or rectum. Stage IVB: Distant metastasis. The primary treatment for uterine LMS is surgical management, typically involving a total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH) with or without bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO), which entails the removal of the fallopian tubes and ovaries. In some cases, pelvic lymphadenectomy (removal of pelvic lymph nodes) and excision of extrauterine disease may also be performed. However, preoperative differentiation between benign and malignant fibroids is often unreliable, leading to a retrospective diagnosis of LMS. Complete surgical excision of the tumor offers the best chance for cure. Nevertheless, due to the likelihood of microscopic metastatic disease at the time of diagnosis, adjuvant therapies are frequently recommended following surgery. Adjuvant treatments may include radiotherapy (RT), chemotherapy, or a combination of both. Commonly used chemotherapy agents include doxorubicin, docetaxel, and gemcitabine. Hormonal therapies have also been explored as they tend to have fewer side effects compared to chemotherapy. For patients presenting with metastatic disease, the focus may shift to best supportive care aimed at improving quality of life, as active treatments are unlikely to significantly extend survival. For patients with LMS confined to the uterus at the time of surgery, total hysterectomy is the standard recommendation. Studies have demonstrated that achieving complete cytoreduction (removal of all visible disease) is associated with improved disease-free survival. However, the impact of BSO on survival outcomes remains unclear. In cases where the disease has spread beyond the uterus, the role of surgery is controversial, as it may not provide survival benefits and could potentially cause harm. For patients with disease confined to the pelvis (stage II) or abdomen (stage III), TAH and BSO with cytoreduction of intra-abdominal and retroperitoneal disease are often performed. Although data are limited to small, uncontrolled series, optimal surgical cytoreduction has been associated with improved overall survival compared to cases with residual disease after surgery. However, these studies are subject to significant bias. Lymph node involvement is uncommon in LMS confined to the uterus, as the disease primarily spreads via the bloodstream rather than lymphatic channels. Consequently, pelvic lymphadenectomy may not be necessary. A Gynecologic Oncology Group (GOG) study involving 59 women with clinical stage I or II LMS reported a lymph node metastasis rate of less than 5%. Adjuvant chemotherapy, with or without RT, has been shown to improve progression-free survival (PFS). For example, a randomized trial involving women with stage I and II uterine sarcomas found no significant survival advantage with RT alone after surgery. However, other studies suggest that RT may reduce local recurrence and improve overall survival. The efficacy of adjuvant chemotherapy in improving survival outcomes remains uncertain, although responses to chemotherapy in recurrent disease have been documented. Between 30% and 50% of women with high-grade LMS confined to the uterus remain progression-free at two years. The SARC005 phase 2 trial evaluated the use of adjuvant gemcitabine plus docetaxel followed by doxorubicin in women with LMS. The study reported that 78% of participants were progression-free at two years, and 57% were progression-free at three years. For patients with advanced disease at presentation (stage III or IV), a systematic review of 27 studies, including three randomized controlled trials, concluded that chemotherapy is a reasonable option for palliative care to alleviate symptoms. Among available agents, doxorubicin is preferred, although cisplatin and ifosfamide have also been used, albeit with significant toxicity. Uterine LMS is characterized by high recurrence rates following initial surgery, likely due to the presence of microscopic metastatic disease. This underscores the need for effective adjuvant treatments to reduce recurrence and improve survival. However, there is no consensus on the optimal use of chemotherapy and radiotherapy in early-stage, advanced, or metastatic disease. Given the high toxicity associated with adjuvant treatments, it is crucial to weigh the potential benefits against the risks, particularly when the survival benefits are modest.
